content.overview: Specialist instruction for propagation contamination pathways & layered biosecurity in propagation and clean-stock operations.

sections.title: Propagation concentrates biological risk
sections.body: Donor plants, fresh wounds, repeated handling, shared tools and high plant density create multiple opportunities for pests and pathogens to move through propagation systems. A pathway map helps separate plausible routes from unsupported assumptions.

sections.title: Asymptomatic appearance is not a clean-stock test
sections.body: HLVd can occur without obvious symptoms, so visual inspection alone cannot establish pathogen-free status. Identity, testing context and biosecurity records remain important even when plants appear healthy.

sections.title: Layered controls interrupt pathways
sections.body: Stock separation, controlled movement, tool/work-surface sanitation, source records and testing escalation reduce risk through different mechanisms. No single layer proves a propagation area is biologically clean.

commonMistakes: Treating visible plant health as proof of clean-stock status.
Assuming one sanitation step controls every transmission pathway.
Mapping a possible pathway as if it proves the source of an actual event.
content.practicalApplication: Create a propagation pathway map from donor area through cutting, tray, rooting and handoff; mark movement, tool, water/root-zone and personnel interfaces plus the evidence needed to investigate each.
content.summary: Biosecurity begins with identifying plausible movement pathways and applying multiple controls without overstating what any single control proves.
